kinds.d: Plagioclase feldspar mineral specimen showing labradorescence, a blue-green-gold iridescent schiller; sold as rough, slabs and cabochons.

x.d: Highly iridescent labradorite from Ylämaa, Finland, showing pink, orange and purple flashes; the name is a brand name for Finnish material.

v.n: Ylämaa deposit found by Pekka Laitakari
First Ylämaa workshop cutting spectrolite for jewellery

x.d: Type-area labradorite from Paul's Island near Nain, Labrador, Canada.
Major source of mainly blue-grey-green labradorite.

kinds.d: Potassium feldspar mineral specimen: white to cream crystals, the green variety being amazonite.

x.d: Green microcline; despite the name it is not found in the Amazon Basin.
Microcline or orthoclase with thin exsolved albite layers.
Microcline from St Gotthard, Mt Greiner (Zillertal) and Baveno, Piedmont.
Microcline from the Pikes Peak area and Crystal Peak, Colorado.
Microcline from the Ilmen Mountains, Urals.

kinds.d: Potassium feldspar mineral specimen: Carlsbad-twinned crystals; adularia and moonstone are gem varieties.

x.d: Low-temperature feldspar first reported from the Adula Alps, Switzerland, described by Pini in 1781.
Gem intergrowth of orthoclase and albite showing adularescence.
Higher-temperature polymorph in rapidly cooled volcanic rocks.
Typical twinning of orthoclase; classic Carlsbad (Bohemia) crystals.
Gem crystals from Ampandrandava and Itrongay, Madagascar.

kinds.d: Sodium feldspar mineral specimen: white, striated crystals and platy cleavelandite.

x.d: Platy, bladed albite from granitic pegmatites.
Iridescent albite from the White Sea coast, identified in 1925 by Alexander Fersman.
Albite from St Gotthard, Tavetsch, Roc Tournée (Savoie) and Mt Greiner.
Albite from the Pala and Mesa Grande districts, San Diego County.

kinds.d: Deep blue metamorphic rock of lazurite with calcite and pyrite, and the feldspathoid lazurite itself; rough, cabochons and carvings.

x.d: Lapis from the Sar-i Sang mines in the Kokcha valley, Badakhshan, Afghanistan, worked for more than 6,000 years.
Lapis from Ovalle, Chile, paler and often with calcite.
Lapis from the Tultui deposit west of Lake Baikal, Russia.
Pigment from ground lapis used in Renaissance and Baroque painting until synthetic ultramarine replaced it in the early 19th century.
Well-crystallised lazurite from Sar-e-Sang and Slyudyanka, Lake Baikal.

kinds.d: Sodium aluminium silicate chloride mineral specimen: royal blue masses with white veins; hackmanite changes colour in light.

x.d: Blue sodalite from the Princess Sodalite Mine, Bancroft, Ontario.
Tenebrescent sodalite: violet when freshly quarried at Mont Saint-Hilaire and Greenland and fading to grey; Afghan and Myanmar material turns violet to pink-red in sunlight.
Type-locality sodalite from the Ilimaussaq intrusion, Greenland, first described in 1811.
Transparent sodalite crystals from northern Namibia.
Smaller deposits in Brazil.

kinds.d: Sodium calcium aluminium silicate sulfate mineral specimen: bright blue grains and rare gem crystals from volcanic rocks.

x.d: Blue haüyne in ejected hornblende-haüyne-scapolite rock from the Laacher See complex, Eifel, Germany.
Type-locality haüyne from Lake Nemi, Alban Hills, Italy; named by Brunn-Neergard in 1807.
Haüyne from Monte Somma and Vesuvius lavas.
Rare faceted blue haüyne.

notes: All 7 planned kinds kept (kind 'Lapis lazuli and lazurite' covers both rock and mineral). Sources: Wikipedia and HOM (microcline, orthoclase, albite, lazurite, sodalite, hauyne). Not on fetched pages and omitted: Pikes Peak amazonite colour cause, peristerite, moonstone localities. No brands or traditions.
